paragraphs: A word’s useful representation can depend on the words around it. This paper develops a probabilistic sequence model that produces continuous word representations incorporating local context. Each representation is the posterior mean of a hidden state in a linear dynamical system: an estimate of that state after accounting for the observed text.

The linear structure makes inference efficient through Kalman filtering. Learning also uses a compact source of information: word co-occurrence counts support both initialization by the method of moments and subsequent expectation-maximization updates. This connects contextual word representations to a sequence-modeling approach whose training procedure is designed to scale.

The inferred representations improve accuracy when used as features in the reported tagging experiments. The authors also interpret Kalman-filter updates as a linear recurrent neural network and use learned parameters to initialize a nonlinear recurrent language model. In that experiment, initialization cuts training time by a day and lowers perplexity. The results therefore demonstrate uses both as contextual features and as a starting point for another model.
icml-2015-a-linear-dynamical-system-mode.tldr: A linear dynamical model learns contextual word representations efficiently and provides useful features and initialization for language models.

paragraphs: A visualization can emphasize broad categories or finer distinctions within them. This paper investigates how the divergence measure used in nonlinear dimensionality reduction influences that emphasis. Its method generalizes t-SNE through an alpha-beta divergence, whose two parameters can favor large-scale organization or more detailed classes.

The authors combine theoretical analysis with experiments across ten datasets. Their analysis identifies parameter choices that reveal these different levels of structure across datasets, reducing the need for extensive parameter grid searches. The contribution is therefore more than another visualization objective: it explains how particular choices affect the kinds of relationships a visualization exposes.

The paper also develops parallel CPU and GPU implementations, addressing tree-based optimization and datasets too large to fit entirely in GPU memory. It reports a twentyfold speedup over the fastest published implementation used for comparison. Case studies include image and particle-physics datasets containing up to eleven million instances. These results connect control over visual structure with the computational ability to explore very large collections.
icml-2015-alpha-beta-divergences-discove.tldr: A generalization of t-SNE uses alpha-beta divergence parameters to reveal broad or fine-grained structure while supporting large-scale visualization.

paragraphs: Transfer learning uses information from a source task to help a target task. This paper proposes a Bayesian approach based on a two-layer deep Gaussian process. The transfer is asymmetric: the target learner draws on the source representation while also keeping a representation specific to its own domain.

The first layer maps each task’s data onto a separate nonlinear manifold, providing different representation spaces for the source and target. To transfer knowledge, the model additionally maps target data onto the source manifold. It then linearly combines the target data’s representations in both spaces. This gives the target learner access to source-domain structure without requiring it to rely exclusively on that structure.

The reported evaluations cover a real-world image categorization benchmark and tumor detection across tissue types in histopathology images. The approach reaches state-of-the-art performance on the categorization benchmark and improves on it in the tumor-detection setting. These findings support the usefulness of combining source and target representations in the evaluated tasks, rather than establishing that such transfer benefits every pair of domains.
icml-2015-asymmetric-transfer-learning-w.tldr: A deep Gaussian process transfers knowledge by combining target data’s representations in separate source and target spaces.

paragraphs: BilBOWA learns word vectors for two languages using large monolingual text collections alongside a smaller bilingual resource. Its training does not require individual words to be matched across languages. It does require sentence-aligned text, which supplies the connection between the two languages without specifying exactly which words translate one another.

The model combines two noise-contrastive language models with a sampled cross-language bag-of-words objective. The language models learn from monolingual data, while the additional objective regularizes them using the bilingual signal. In this way, sentence-level correspondence helps shape word representations across languages while the larger monolingual collections contribute information within each language.

The authors emphasize computational efficiency and the ability to scale to large monolingual datasets. They evaluate the resulting embeddings on cross-language document classification and lexical translation using WMT11 data, reporting improvements over state-of-the-art methods. These results show that the coarser sentence-alignment signal can support useful bilingual word representations in the tested tasks, without the word-level alignment requirement that the method was designed to remove.
icml-2015-bilbowa-fast-bilingual-distrib.tldr: BilBOWA efficiently learns bilingual word vectors from monolingual text and sentence-aligned data without requiring word alignments.

paragraphs: The cascade model describes a user inspecting an ordered list and selecting the first attractive item. This paper turns that behavior model into a learning problem: identify the K most attractive items through repeated interactions. Because selection depends on where the user stops, the learner receives only partial information about the displayed list.

The authors formulate this as a stochastic combinatorial partial-monitoring problem and introduce CascadeUCB1 and CascadeKL-UCB. They analyze regret, which measures the cost of learning rather than consistently making the best choices. Their upper bounds depend on gaps between item qualities, connecting learning difficulty to how clearly attractive items can be distinguished.

A lower bound describes unavoidable regret in this problem. It matches the CascadeKL-UCB upper bound up to a logarithmic factor, indicating that the algorithm approaches that theoretical benchmark. Experiments also find strong performance when modeling assumptions are violated. That empirical robustness is encouraging, but it is distinct from extending the stated regret guarantees to those violations.
icml-2015-cascading-bandits-learning-to-.tldr: Two cascading-bandit algorithms learn attractive ranked items from partial feedback, with regret guarantees and encouraging empirical robustness.

paragraphs: Online systems often record feedback only for the choices they actually presented, such as clicks on displayed advertisements. Learning a new decision rule from those records is counterfactual: the records do not directly show what would have happened under alternative choices. This paper develops a principle and algorithm for learning from such logged bandit feedback.

The approach uses propensity scoring to address how the original system selected its actions. It then derives generalization bounds that explicitly account for the variance of the resulting weighted empirical-risk estimate. These bounds motivate Counterfactual Risk Minimization, connecting the learning objective to both estimated performance and uncertainty in that estimate.

The authors instantiate the principle as POEM, a method for learning stochastic linear rules with structured outputs. A decomposition of its objective supports efficient stochastic-gradient optimization. Evaluations on several multilabel classification problems show substantially improved robustness and generalization relative to the compared state-of-the-art methods. The findings support variance-aware learning from logged feedback in those experiments.
icml-2015-counterfactual-risk-minimizati.tldr: Counterfactual Risk Minimization combines propensity weighting with variance-aware bounds to learn more robust decision rules from logged feedback.

paragraphs: Subspace clustering groups observations that lie approximately within several affine subspaces. The challenge includes deciding how many subspaces are needed and how many dimensions each should have. This paper introduces a Bayesian nonparametric model that infers both quantities from observed data, allowing different clusters to have different dimensional complexity.

Direct posterior inference is difficult, so the authors use small-variance asymptotics to derive a deterministic algorithm called DP-space. The resulting procedure retains the ability to infer the number and dimensions of subspaces. Its objective explicitly balances how well the subspaces fit the data against the complexity of the resulting model.

DP-space decreases this objective monotonically, providing a clear optimization criterion for its updates. That property describes improvement of the objective rather than a claim of finding a global optimum. Experiments report better clustering accuracy than several competing methods while also showing high efficiency. The contribution therefore combines adaptive model structure with a practical optimization procedure and favorable results on the evaluated clustering problems.
icml-2015-dp-space-bayesian-nonparametri.tldr: DP-space efficiently learns both the number and dimensions of clustering subspaces by balancing data fit against model complexity.

paragraphs: Fictitious play is a model of learning in games, but applying it to large problems can be computationally demanding. This paper develops two variants expressed through behavioral strategies in extensive-form games. That representation describes decisions within the game’s unfolding structure and provides a basis for making fictitious play more practical.

The first variant is a full-width procedure that is realization equivalent to its normal-form counterpart. This equivalence lets it inherit that counterpart’s convergence guarantees. Its time and space requirements are linear rather than exponential, making the representation change consequential for computation as well as for the connection to existing theory.

The second variant, Fictitious Self-Play, implements fictitious play through a sample-based machine-learning framework. The authors compare the approaches experimentally in poker games with imperfect information and demonstrate convergence to approximate Nash equilibria. The evidence thus has two distinct parts: inherited guarantees for the equivalent full-width procedure and experimental convergence results for the evaluated approaches. The abstract does not claim universal convergence for every game.
icml-2015-fictitious-self-play-in-extens.tldr: Two extensive-form variants make fictitious play more practical, with inherited guarantees for one and approximate-equilibrium results in poker experiments.

paragraphs: Text-based cascades connect documents or posts through events such as retweeting or publishing a follow-up. Understanding them involves both the subject matter of the text and the pathways through which information spreads. HawkesTopic brings these two questions into a single model rather than treating topic discovery and diffusion-network inference as separate tasks.

The model combines Hawkes processes with topic modeling. The former component represents the diffusion process, while the latter characterizes the topics in the observed text. A mean-field variational inference algorithm estimates them jointly. The central modeling choice is to reason about textual content and information pathways together within the same inference procedure.

The authors evaluate HawkesTopic on synthetic and real-world data. Their applications include information diffusion among news media and scientific influence in an ArXiv publication dataset. They report significantly greater accuracy than several baselines for both tasks. These results support joint modeling in the tested settings, showing that the combined approach can improve the inference of topics and diffusion pathways.
icml-2015-hawkestopic-a-joint-model-for-.tldr: HawkesTopic jointly infers topics and information-diffusion pathways from text cascades using Hawkes processes and variational inference.

paragraphs: Gaussian-process approximations face a tension between representing complex functions and fitting the data too closely. The paper identifies difficulties with standard sparse pseudo-input methods on complex functions and overfitting in sparse-spectrum alternatives. It proposes a variational treatment of sparse spectra to address both issues within the same approximation.

The covariance function is represented by a finite Fourier-series approximation and treated as a random quantity. Instead of relying on a single fixed covariance function, the method places a variational distribution over its posterior. Fitting this distribution adapts the random covariance function to the observations while explicitly representing uncertainty in the spectral approximation.

The authors investigate the approximation’s properties, compare it with other inference approaches, and extend it to distributed and stochastic settings. They report better capture of complex functions than standard approaches while avoiding overfitting. The contribution is the combination of a compact spectral representation and uncertainty-aware inference, with extensions that make the approach relevant to more than one computational training setting.
icml-2015-improving-the-gaussian-process.tldr: Variational uncertainty over a sparse Fourier covariance approximation helps Gaussian processes capture complex functions while avoiding overfitting.

paragraphs: Markov jump processes model phenomena involving changes between states, including disease progression and RNA folding. The paper addresses two difficulties in existing inference methods: degenerate trajectories from maximum-likelihood estimation of parametric models, and poor inference performance in nonparametric models. Its proposed route is to derive small-variance asymptotic formulations of these processes.

The derivations cover both parametric and nonparametric models, with either directly observed or hidden states. For parametric models, the resulting objective produces nondegenerate trajectories. For the nonparametric formulation, the authors introduce a gamma-gamma process that extends the gamma-exponential process. They then provide algorithms for the different formulations under the shared name JUMP-means.

Experiments compare JUMP-means with widely used Markov-jump-process inference approaches on speed and reconstruction accuracy. The reported performance is competitive with or better than those alternatives. This qualified result matters: the paper presents an effective family of inference procedures across several formulations, rather than claiming that every variant dominates every comparison. Its methodological contribution links asymptotic analysis to concrete inference objectives and algorithms.
icml-2015-jump-means-small-variance-asym.tldr: JUMP-means derives practical Markov-jump-process inference algorithms with nondegenerate parametric trajectories and competitive speed and reconstruction accuracy.

paragraphs: Vectors of categorical variables have a rapidly growing number of possible combinations. A dataset may cover only a small fraction of them, making distribution estimation difficult. This paper tackles that sparsity with an unsupervised Bayesian model that represents observations through a continuous latent space, allowing similarities between categorical combinations to inform the model.

The model generates categorical vectors through a nonlinear transformation of that latent space. The continuous representation addresses sparse coverage, while nonlinearity allows the distribution to have multiple modes, or distinct concentrations of probability. The construction connects linear categorical latent Gaussian models, Gaussian-process latent-variable models, and Gaussian-process classification within a common modeling approach.

The authors derive inference using sampling-based variational methods and evaluate the model through missing-value imputation on sparse data. It empirically outperforms the linear and discrete counterparts used in those comparisons. These results support the usefulness of combining continuous representations with nonlinear modeling when estimating missing categorical values; the stated evidence concerns those imputation tasks rather than every use of categorical data.
icml-2015-latent-gaussian-processes-for-.tldr: A nonlinear Bayesian latent-space model estimates sparse categorical distributions and improves imputation over its tested linear and discrete counterparts.

paragraphs: Researchers often need topic models tailored to a particular question, especially in the social sciences and humanities. Building those models individually requires substantial design effort and technical expertise. This paper introduces latent topic networks as a flexible family of structured topic models intended to make such customization more accessible within a common framework.

Users express custom models through a probabilistic programming language based on first-order logic. This provides a way to specify richer topic-model structure without designing a wholly separate framework for each application. Training uses a parallelizable expectation-maximization algorithm, with ADMM handling the maximization step, connecting modeling flexibility to a scalable computational procedure.

The paper demonstrates the framework through case studies involving influence in citation networks and presidential State of the Union addresses. These applications illustrate its ability to accommodate different research questions and text collections. The central contribution is a reusable route from structured model specification to training, with the case studies supporting broad applicability rather than establishing a single predictive advantage across all topic-modeling tasks.
icml-2015-latent-topic-networks-a-versat.tldr: Latent topic networks combine logical probabilistic programming with parallelizable training to support customized, richly structured topic models.

paragraphs: Symmetric positive definite matrices can represent image sets, and Log-Euclidean methods work with their matrix logarithms. Existing approaches commonly convert those logarithms into vectors. The paper argues that this conversion distorts the geometry of the matrix-logarithm space and becomes inefficient when the matrices have many dimensions.

The proposed method learns directly from the matrix logarithms. It seeks a tangent map that transforms them from their original tangent space into another space intended to better distinguish classes. This makes the learned transformation responsible for improving discriminability while keeping the learning formulation tied to matrix-valued representations.

Within that framework, learning becomes an optimization problem over a Mahalanobis-like matrix, allowing the approach to draw on traditional metric-learning techniques. Evaluations across several image-set classification tasks demonstrate the method’s effectiveness. The contribution connects the geometry of the representation to a familiar kind of distance learning, with experimental support for the resulting classification approach rather than a claim that one metric is best for every dataset.
icml-2015-log-euclidean-metric-learning-.tldr: A metric-learning method transforms SPD matrix logarithms directly to improve discrimination in image-set classification.

paragraphs: Low-rank approximation compresses a matrix into a representation that retains a smaller number of dominant directions. It supports tools such as principal component analysis and applications including text mining and computer vision. This paper shows how matrices constructed from error-correcting codes can be used to build such approximations of large matrices.

The proposed code matrices are easy to generate and substantially reduce the amount of randomness needed. Their low coherence supports a better chance of preserving the geometry of a whole subspace. The paper also identifies a sampling advantage: the logarithmic factor in the O(k log k) column requirement for Fourier or Hadamard constructions is unnecessary for the code-matrix approach.

Under certain conditions, code matrices can also produce smaller approximation errors and more accurate singular values than Gaussian and other structured random matrices. That accuracy advantage is conditional, rather than a universal ordering of the methods. Together, the claims make code-based constructions an alternative whose appeal includes reduced randomness, subspace preservation, and potentially better approximation quality.
icml-2015-low-rank-approximation-using-e.tldr: Error-correcting code matrices reduce randomness in low-rank approximation and can improve sampling requirements and, under certain conditions, accuracy.

paragraphs: Collective graphical models reason about populations when observations consist of noisy aggregate information rather than individual records. Their population model assumes independent, identically distributed individuals. This paper develops a more efficient inference method by relating approximate maximum-a-posteriori inference in these collective models to marginal inference in ordinary graphical models.

That connection leads to a belief-propagation-style message-passing algorithm. Mathematically, the procedure strictly generalizes belief propagation: its optimization objective combines the Bethe free energy with additional terms that depend nonlinearly on the marginals. This explains how a familiar graphical-model inference approach can be extended to accommodate the collective setting.

The authors report that the method is much more efficient than previous inference approaches for collective graphical models. They demonstrate performance in two synthetic experiments involving bird migration and collective human mobility. Those examples show the approach working on population-level movement problems, while the synthetic nature of the evaluations distinguishes them from evidence gathered directly from real migrating birds or observed human populations.
icml-2015-message-passing-for-collective.tldr: A generalized belief-propagation algorithm makes collective graphical-model inference more efficient when observations are noisy population aggregates.

paragraphs: When the same subjects have several kinds of measurements, useful clusters may agree across those views while depending on different features in each one. This paper addresses that setting by jointly discovering subject groups and the feature subsets associated with them. It allows the underlying clusters to occupy different subspaces across views.

The proposed algorithm simultaneously decomposes multiple data matrices into sparse row and column vectors. Sparsity supports selecting relevant subjects and features within the decomposition, while the joint formulation maintains consistent subject grouping across views. Optimization uses proximal alternating linearized minimization, providing a procedure for handling these coupled sparse representations.

The convergence result is to a critical point of the optimization problem; it does not establish a globally optimal solution. A simulation study shows recovery of the hypothesized clusters and associated features. Comparisons on benchmark datasets report stronger performance than several recent multi-view co-clustering methods. Together, these findings support learning both shared grouping structure and view-specific feature relevance within one approach.
icml-2015-multi-view-sparse-co-clusterin.tldr: A sparse multi-view co-clustering method jointly discovers consistent subject groups and their view-specific features, with convergence to a critical point.

paragraphs: Before replacing an existing decision policy, it is useful to estimate how a proposed policy would perform. This paper studies that question using observations collected under the existing policy. Its G-SCOPE algorithm evaluates a new policy from those records, addressing the need for evidence about a policy before directly testing it.

G-SCOPE takes a model-based approach and greedily learns to exploit factored structure in the environment’s dynamics. The key idea is that the dynamics have structure that can be used rather than treated as one undifferentiated high-dimensional problem. The paper attributes both computational efficiency and sample efficiency to learning and exploiting those factors.

The authors provide a finite-sample analysis and report experiments in which the algorithm scales well to high-dimensional problems using few samples. These contributions address both the theoretical behavior of evaluation from limited data and its practical computational feasibility. The motivating aim is evidence for policy improvement; the abstract’s concrete contribution is an efficient evaluation algorithm, not a guarantee that any proposed policy is superior.
icml-2015-off-policy-model-based-learnin.tldr: G-SCOPE evaluates a new policy using existing-policy data by efficiently learning and exploiting factored environment dynamics.

paragraphs: Submodular function minimization appears in machine learning and computer vision, but general-purpose methods can be too slow for large problems despite polynomial-time solvability. This paper focuses on functions that decompose into sums of simpler components. That structure creates opportunities for more practical optimization than treating the whole function through a general-purpose algorithm.

The authors use random coordinate descent to develop algorithms with faster linear convergence rates and lower iteration costs. Their comparison is with alternating-projection approaches developed through convex optimization. A central computational distinction is that the new algorithms avoid full-dimensional vector operations, reducing the work involved in individual updates.

The methods also converge in substantially fewer iterations than the alternating-projection comparison. These are complementary improvements: cheaper updates address the cost of each step, while faster convergence addresses how many steps are required. The paper’s contribution is therefore a more efficient optimization route for the decomposable class. Its scope depends on the available sum-of-simple-functions structure rather than asserting the same improvement for arbitrary submodular functions.
icml-2015-random-coordinate-descent-meth.tldr: Random coordinate descent speeds up decomposable submodular minimization through cheaper updates and faster linear convergence.

paragraphs: Pairwise preferences can cycle: one item may beat a second, the second a third, and the third the first. In that setting, minimizing overall pairwise disagreement does not necessarily put desirable winners at the top. This paper studies rankings learned from randomly sampled comparisons with an explicit focus on top-ranked items.

A Condorcet winner, when one exists, beats every other item. More general tournament solution concepts identify sets of winners when cycles prevent such a simple answer. The authors show that existing ranking algorithms can fail to place these winners appropriately, then provide alternative algorithms with provable guarantees for Condorcet winners, top cycles, and other solution sets.

The paper gives finite-sample bounds for recovering the relevant winners, connecting the ranking guarantees to the number of observed comparisons. It also improves the sample-complexity bound for Rank Centrality under the Bradley–Terry–Luce condition. That additional result is conditional on that preference model. Overall, the work distinguishes finding a globally satisfactory ordering from reliably placing specified kinds of winners first.
icml-2015-ranking-from-stochastic-pairwi.tldr: New ranking algorithms provably place Condorcet winners and selected tournament solution sets at the top despite cyclic preferences.

paragraphs: Stochastic dual coordinate ascent solves regularized empirical-risk minimization problems by iteratively updating dual variables. This paper asks whether the probabilities used to choose those variables should change as optimization proceeds. Its AdaSDCA method makes that sampling distribution adaptive, allowing the selection rule to evolve throughout the iterative process.

The theoretical result is a better complexity bound than SDCA using the best fixed probability distribution, known as importance sampling. This comparison is meaningful because the advantage is over an optimized fixed sampling rule. However, the authors explicitly describe AdaSDCA as expensive to implement, so the improved bound does not by itself establish a practical computational advantage.

To address that cost, they introduce AdaSDCA+, a practical variant. In the reported experiments, it outperforms existing nonadaptive methods. The paper thus separates two contributions: a theoretical case for changing sampling probabilities during optimization and an implementable method with empirical benefits. The abstract gives the stronger complexity claim for AdaSDCA and the experimental performance claim for AdaSDCA+.
icml-2015-stochastic-dual-coordinate-asc.tldr: Adaptive coordinate sampling improves SDCA’s theoretical complexity, while a practical variant outperforms nonadaptive methods in experiments.

paragraphs: This paper studies online decisions over a continuous set of possible choices. At each iteration, the decision maker selects a probability distribution over a subset of Euclidean space, then learns the loss function afterward. The aim is to control cumulative expected loss despite having to choose before seeing that iteration’s loss.

The authors generalize Hedge to this setting and prove a regret bound of O(√t log t). The guarantee requires uniformly Lipschitz losses and a uniformly fat decision set. Uniform fatness is weaker than convexity, so the result applies to some nonconvex sets as well. It does not require convexity, but it still depends on a stated geometric condition.

The sublinear growth of the bound means the corresponding regret per iteration decreases as the number of iterations grows under those assumptions. The paper also generalizes dual averaging to Lebesgue-continuous distributions over the decision set. Together, the contributions extend distribution-based online optimization to continuous domains while making explicit the regularity conditions supporting the regret guarantee.
icml-2015-the-hedge-algorithm-on-a-conti.tldr: A continuous-domain Hedge algorithm achieves O(√t log t) regret under uniform Lipschitz and geometric fatness assumptions.

paragraphs: The paper studies sparse-signal recovery in one-bit compressed sensing and proposes an algorithm using a nonconvex penalty that encourages sparsity. Its main result relates the required number of observations to signal strength, the number of nonzero entries s, the full dimension d, and the desired recovery error ε.

For strong signals, the proven sample complexity is O(s/ε²), removing the logarithmic dimension factor from the stated previous best bound. For weak signals, the bound is O(s log d/ε²). General signals fall between these expressions. The improvement therefore depends on signal strength; the strongest bound is not presented as applying uniformly to every signal.

For strong signals, the authors also establish exact support recovery with high probability, meaning recovery of which entries are nonzero. This is distinct from merely approximating the signal’s values. Numerical experiments in noisy settings support the theory and demonstrate advantages for both approximate signal recovery and support recovery. The work connects a sparsity-inducing optimization choice to strength-dependent guarantees and empirical recovery performance.
icml-2015-towards-a-lower-sample-complex.tldr: A nonconvex sparsity-based algorithm improves one-bit sensing sample complexity for strong signals and recovers their support with high probability.

paragraphs: The paper learns video representations by asking a sequence model to reconstruct observed frames or predict future ones. An encoder LSTM compresses an input sequence into a fixed-length representation. One or more decoder LSTMs then use that representation for these tasks, providing a way to learn from video without action labels.

Experiments use both image-pixel patches and higher-level frame representations extracted by a pretrained convolutional network. The authors examine design choices, including whether a decoder should condition on its generated outputs. Qualitative analysis explores how the learned representation supports extending a sequence into the future or reconstructing information about the past.

To test usefulness for recognition, the representations are fine-tuned on human-action classification using UCF-101 and HMDB-51. They improve classification accuracy, particularly when training examples are scarce. Pretraining on an unrelated collection of 300 hours of YouTube video can also help. These results indicate that the sequence-learning tasks can produce transferable representations in the evaluated settings, including when labeled action data are limited.
icml-2015-unsupervised-learning-of-video.tldr: LSTM reconstruction and prediction learn transferable video representations that improve action recognition, especially with limited labeled examples.

paragraphs: This paper broadens undirected graphical models so that an individual variable can take values in an arbitrary vector space. Its Vector-Space Markov Random Fields extend earlier scalar-valued exponential-family and mixed graphical models. This enlargement makes additional distribution families available, including multinomial and Dirichlet distributions.

The models are characterized through their node-conditional distributions: each variable’s distribution, given the others, belongs to a generic exponential family on a vector-space domain. The authors also introduce an estimator for learning the graph. Its sparsistency result means that it recovers the correct edge set with high probability, providing a theoretical statement about learning dependence structure.

Validation includes synthetic experiments and a case study involving more than four million foods from MyFitnessPal. The reported results show good empirical performance and the ability to expose interesting structure in complex data. The contribution combines a broader class of allowable variables with a graph-learning method, supported by both a probabilistic edge-recovery guarantee and evidence from the evaluated datasets.
icml-2015-vector-space-markov-random-fie.tldr: Vector-Space Markov Random Fields broaden graphical modeling to vector-valued variables and provide an estimator with high-probability edge recovery.
